paraphrase: If you are attached to this life, you are not a dharma practitioner.
notes: Line wording recalled; the Tibetan of line 2 is given variously as 'khor ba' or 'khams gsum'. Sakya teachers correlate the lines with the three scopes and the view.

paraphrase: If you are attached to saṃsāra (the three realms), you do not have renunciation.
notes: Line wording recalled; the Tibetan of line 2 is given variously as 'khor ba' or 'khams gsum'. Sakya teachers correlate the lines with the three scopes and the view.

paraphrase: If you are attached to your own purpose, you do not have the mind of awakening.
notes: Line wording recalled; the Tibetan of line 2 is given variously as 'khor ba' or 'khams gsum'. Sakya teachers correlate the lines with the three scopes and the view.

paraphrase: If grasping arises, you do not have the view.
notes: Line wording recalled; the Tibetan of line 2 is given variously as 'khor ba' or 'khams gsum'. Sakya teachers correlate the lines with the three scopes and the view.

location.section: the tradition's account of the revelation

paraphrase: At twelve, during a six-month retreat on Mañjuśrī under Bari Lotsawa, Sachen Kunga Nyingpo saw Mañjuśrī, who spoke the four lines of Parting from the Four Attachments; Sachen understood that the whole of the path of the perfections is contained in them.
notes: Hagiographical narrative, not a line of the text.

paraphrase: Ethics, study, reflection and meditation practised for this life's sake are without essence: ethics kept for this life is the root of the lower realms, study and reflection so done are the root of pride and dispute, meditation so done is only a basis for worldly distraction — so do not be attached to this life.
notes: Paraphrase of the song's argument for each line, recalled in outline only; not a verse-level record.

paraphrase: Reflecting on the sufferings of the three lower realms, of the gods and humans, and on the change and pervasive suffering of all saṃsāra, there is no happiness in it; so give up attachment to the three realms.
notes: Paraphrase of the song's argument for each line, recalled in outline only; not a verse-level record.

paraphrase: Liberating only oneself is useless when all beings of the three realms have been one's parents; generate the mind of awakening for them, taking on their suffering and giving them one's happiness.
notes: Paraphrase of the song's argument for each line, recalled in outline only; not a verse-level record.

paraphrase: There is no liberation for one who clings to existence, no higher rebirth for one who clings to non-existence, and clinging to both is ignorance; rest free of extremes in the natural state beyond elaboration.
notes: Paraphrase of the song's argument for each line, recalled in outline only; not a verse-level record.

paraphrase: Having gained this precious human life with its freedoms and endowments, so hard to find, to free oneself and others from the ocean of saṃsāra, listening, reflecting and meditating day and night without distraction is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: In one's homeland attachment to friends surges like water, hatred of enemies burns like fire, and the darkness of ignorance forgets what to adopt and reject; to give up one's homeland is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: Long-accompanying friends and relatives will separate, wealth gained with effort will be left behind, and consciousness, a guest, will leave the guest-house of the body; to give up concern for this life is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: The companion with whom the three poisons grow, hearing, reflection and meditation decline, and love and compassion are lost — to abandon such bad friends is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: The spiritual friend through whom one's faults are exhausted and good qualities grow like the waxing moon — to cherish him more than one's own body is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: Worldly gods, themselves bound in the prison of saṃsāra, whom can they protect? To go for refuge to the Three Jewels, which do not deceive, is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: When the mothers who have loved one from beginningless time are suffering, what use is one's own happiness? To generate the mind of awakening to free limitless beings is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: All suffering without exception comes from wanting happiness for oneself; the perfect Buddhas arise from the mind intent on others' good; truly to exchange one's own happiness for others' suffering is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: Even if someone should cut off one's head though one has done no wrong, through the power of compassion to take their wrongdoing upon oneself is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: If one does not subdue the enemy of one's own anger, the more outer enemies one conquers the more they will increase; to subdue one's own mind with the army of love and compassion is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: Sense pleasures are like salt water: the more one indulges, the more craving grows; to give up at once whatever arouses attachment is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: Whatever appears is one's own mind, and the nature of mind is from the beginning free of elaboration; knowing this, not to attend to the marks of subject and object is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: Knowing that insight joined with calm abiding completely destroys the afflictions, to cultivate the concentration that fully transcends the four formless absorptions is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: Without wisdom the five perfections cannot bring perfect awakening; to cultivate wisdom joined with method, not conceptualising the three spheres, is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: When afflictions become habitual, antidotes are hard to apply; with the weapons of mindfulness and alertness to destroy afflictions like attachment the moment they arise is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: In short, wherever one is and whatever one does, examining the state of one's mind and, with constant mindfulness and alertness, accomplishing the good of others is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: To dedicate the virtue produced by such effort to dispelling the suffering of limitless beings, with wisdom purified of the three spheres, is the practice of a bodhisattva.
notes: Recalled; verse numbers follow the standard 37-verse count (homage and promise not counted).

paraphrase: As peacocks roam the forest of poisonous plants and thrive on poison where other birds would die, so bodhisattvas remain in the jungle of saṃsāra and turn the poisonous afflictions into the path.
notes: Section-level ref (the opening simile); verse numbers not recalled.

paraphrase: Whatever misfortune befalls one is the wheel of sharp weapons of one's own wrong deeds turning back upon oneself; so turn the weapon on the true enemy, the demon of self-grasping and self-cherishing, and trample it.
notes: Paraphrase of the poem's refrain-theme; verse numbers not recalled.

paraphrase: Seeing that self-cherishing is the door to all unwanted suffering and that cherishing one's mothers is the basis of all good qualities, bless me to make the yoga of exchanging self and others the heart of my practice.
notes: Section-level ref (the lamrim verses of the Guru Pūjā); verse number not given.

paraphrase: Therefore, compassionate venerable teachers, bless me that all the wrongdoing, obscurations and suffering of mother beings ripen on me right now, and that by giving my happiness and virtue to others all beings may be happy.
notes: Section-level ref; wording recalled.

paraphrase: The teaching of the stages of the path has four greatnesses: through it one understands all the teachings as free of contradiction; all the scriptures dawn as personal instructions; one easily finds the Conqueror's intent; and one is saved from the great wrong of abandoning the dharma.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The root of the path is proper reliance on the spiritual teacher in thought and deed. The qualified teacher of the Mahāyāna has ten qualities (after the Mahāyānasūtrālaṅkāra): disciplined, serene, thoroughly pacified, having more good qualities than the student, energetic, rich in scripture, realized in reality, skilled in speech, loving, and free of weariness in teaching.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: How to conduct a meditation session: the six preparatory practices (cleaning the place and setting up images, arranging offerings, sitting in the proper posture with refuge and bodhicitta, visualizing the field of merit, offering the seven limbs and the maṇḍala, and making requests); then the main topic of meditation; then dedication; between sessions, guarding the senses, eating moderately and so on.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Some claim that all conceptual analysis obstructs meditation and that one should only rest the mind without thought; this is mistaken. Topics such as faith, the value of the human life, impermanence and bodhicitta must be cultivated by analytical meditation that repeatedly examines with discernment, while calm abiding is cultivated by placement meditation; both are meditation.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Contemplate the human life of leisure and endowment — free of the eight unfree states and possessing the ten endowments — its great value (for temporary and final aims), and how difficult it is to find (by its causes, by example and by number); then resolve to take its essence.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Mindfulness of death: death is certain (nothing can stop the Lord of Death, life cannot be extended and continuously runs out, and even while alive there is little time for dharma); the time of death is uncertain (lifespan in this world is not fixed, the causes of death are many and of life few, the body is fragile); at death nothing but dharma helps (not wealth, friends or body). Hence resolve to practise, to practise now, and to practise purely.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Reflect on the sufferings of the hells, the hungry ghosts and animals as where one will go after death if one does not practise.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Going for refuge arises from two causes — fear of the lower realms and faith that the Three Jewels can protect; one knows the qualities of Buddha, Dharma and Saṅgha, goes for refuge by knowing their differences, by commitment, and without speaking of other refuges, and keeps the precepts of refuge.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Karma has four general characteristics: it is certain (virtue brings happiness, non-virtue suffering), it grows greatly, one does not meet the result of what one has not done, and what is done is not lost. The ten non-virtuous paths and their fully-ripened, cause-similar and environmental results are to be understood, and wrongdoing purified by the four powers (repudiation/regret, reliance, the remedy, and restraint from repeating).
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The person of middling scope contemplates the sufferings of saṃsāra in general — the eight sufferings (birth, ageing, sickness, death, meeting the unpleasant, separation from the pleasant, not getting what one wants, the appropriated aggregates), the six sufferings (uncertainty, insatiability, repeatedly discarding bodies, repeatedly taking rebirth, repeated high and low, loneliness) and the three sufferings (of pain, of change, and pervasive conditioning) — and the particular sufferings of each realm.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The origin of suffering: the afflictions — six root afflictions (attachment, anger, pride, ignorance, doubt, afflicted view) — how they arise from the innate grasping at a self, and how through them karma is accumulated; then how one dies and is reborn through the twelve links.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: When, having contemplated the faults of saṃsāra, one wishes for liberation day and night as a prisoner wishes to escape prison, the mind of renunciation (definite emergence) has arisen.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The path that leads to liberation is the three trainings — ethics, concentration and wisdom — of which ethics is the foundation; one guards it by relying on knowledge of the precepts, a pure mind, shame and conscience, and respect.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The only door to the Mahāyāna is the mind of awakening: when it arises one becomes a bodhisattva even without other qualities, and when it is lost one falls from the Mahāyāna even with them; so its benefits must be contemplated.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The sevenfold instruction of cause and effect, from Atiśa's lineage: on the basis of equanimity, (1) recognising all beings as one's mothers, (2) remembering their kindness, (3) wishing to repay it, (4) love, (5) compassion, (6) the extraordinary resolve to take responsibility oneself, and (7) the mind of awakening — the first six being causes and the seventh the effect.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The training in equalizing and exchanging self and other, taught by Śāntideva: considering the faults of self-cherishing and the benefits of cherishing others, one exchanges the objects of cherishing — cherishing others as one used to cherish oneself.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Having trained the mind, adopt the aspiring mind of awakening by ritual, and guard it by the precepts (remembering its benefits, generating it six times a day, not abandoning beings, gathering the accumulations, and abandoning the four black and adopting the four white dharmas).
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Having generated bodhicitta, take the bodhisattva vow and train in the deeds: the six perfections to ripen one's own continuum and the four ways of gathering to ripen others.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Both calm abiding and insight are needed: calm abiding is a mind stably placed on its object without distraction, insight is the wisdom analysing the object; like a lamp that is both bright and unflickering, the view of reality needs both.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The prerequisites of calm abiding are living in a suitable place, having few desires, contentment, not having many activities, pure ethics, and completely abandoning conceptual thoughts such as desire.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Calm abiding is achieved by abandoning the five faults — laziness, forgetting the instruction, laxity and excitement, non-application (of the antidote), and over-application — through the eight antidotes: faith, aspiration, effort and pliancy (against laziness), mindfulness, introspective alertness, application, and equanimity.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The nine mental states are achieved in order: placing the mind, continuous placement, repeated placement, close placement, taming, pacifying, thorough pacifying, one-pointedness and equipoise; by six powers (hearing, reflection, mindfulness, alertness, effort and complete familiarity) and four attentions (tight focus, interrupted, uninterrupted and spontaneous).
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Subtle laxity — where the mind stays on its object with some clarity but its intensity of clarity has slackened — is hard to recognise and is often mistaken for flawless meditation; meditating in it long makes the mind dull and forgetful, and it must be recognised and removed by alertness.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Calm abiding is achieved only when, after the ninth state, mental and then physical pliancy arise with their joy and, that joy settling, the mind rests stably on its object at will; before that one has only a likeness of calm abiding.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Calm abiding alone does not cut the root of saṃsāra — even non-Buddhist sages attain it and still are reborn; the root, grasping at self, is cut only by the wisdom that realizes selflessness.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: To find the view one must rely on the definitive scriptures and on Nāgārjuna's treatises as explained by Buddhapālita and Candrakīrti, whose Prāsaṅgika reading is the final intent.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Just as, to know that a person is absent, one must know the person who is absent, so to realise selflessness one must first correctly identify the self that is to be negated; the object of negation is inherent existence — existence by way of the object's own nature, not posited by the force of conceptual designation. If this is not identified, one's negation will either go too far or not far enough.
notes: Tsongkhapa cites Bodhicaryāvatāra 9.140 ('without contacting the imagined thing, its non-existence is not apprehended'); that verse is not yet a teaching entry in U40. Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Those who negate too much — holding that Madhyamaka reasoning refutes all existence, cause and effect and valid cognition, so that nothing at all can be asserted — fall into nihilism and cannot establish the path; reasoning analysing the ultimate does not find things, but not being found by such reasoning is not the same as being refuted by it.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Those who negate too little — refuting only a self or entity imagined by philosophical systems while leaving the innate apprehension of inherent existence untouched — cannot cut the root of saṃsāra.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The Svātantrikas accept that things have an own-character (inherent nature) conventionally and therefore use autonomous inferences whose subject appears alike to both parties; the Prāsaṅgikas accept no inherent nature even conventionally, so no subject is established in that way and they lead the opponent to the view by consequences and inferences 'renowned to the other'.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: The selflessness of persons is established by the sevenfold reasoning of the chariot: the self is neither one with nor different from the aggregates, neither their possessor, support nor supported, neither their collection nor their shape — yet it exists as merely designated in dependence on them.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Things lack inherent existence yet exist conventionally as mere designations; because they are dependently arisen they are empty, and because they are empty they can function — the emptiness of inherent existence and the working of cause and effect are one meaning.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Insight proper is achieved when analytical meditation on selflessness itself induces pliancy, just as placement induced it in calm abiding; when analysis and stabilization are balanced so that analysis enhances stability, calm abiding and insight are united.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: After training in the paths common to sūtra and tantra, one should certainly enter the Vajrayāna, which is far superior to the other vehicles; one then receives empowerment from a qualified master, guards the vows and commitments as one's life, and trains in the two stages.
notes: Section-level reference (topic of the treatise), recalled; no page or folio.

paraphrase: Paying homage to the venerable teachers, I shall explain as best I can the essence of all the Conqueror's teachings, the path praised by the holy ones, the entrance for fortunate ones seeking liberation; you who are not attached to saṃsāra's pleasures, who strive to make leisure and endowment meaningful and rely on the path that pleases the Conquerors — listen with a clear mind.
notes: Recalled; verse numbering per the common 14-verse division.

paraphrase: Without pure renunciation there is no way to calm the pursuit of pleasures in the ocean of existence; since embodied beings are bound by craving for existence, first seek renunciation.
notes: Recalled; verse numbering per the common 14-verse division.

paraphrase: Leisure and endowment are hard to find and life has no time to spare — accustoming the mind to this reverses attachment to this life; repeatedly thinking of the infallibility of karma and its results and of saṃsāra's sufferings reverses attachment to future lives.
notes: Recalled; verse numbering per the common 14-verse division.

paraphrase: When, having meditated so, not even a moment's wish for saṃsāra's splendours arises and the mind seeks liberation day and night, renunciation has arisen.
notes: Recalled; verse numbering per the common 14-verse division.

paraphrase: Renunciation not held by pure bodhicitta does not become the cause of unsurpassed awakening's perfect bliss; therefore the wise generate the supreme mind of awakening.
notes: Recalled; verse numbering per the common 14-verse division.

paraphrase: Swept by the currents of the four powerful rivers, bound by the tight bonds of karma hard to undo, caught in the iron net of self-grasping, enveloped by the thick darkness of ignorance, endlessly born and reborn in existence and tormented without pause by the three sufferings — thinking of the mothers in this condition, generate the supreme mind.
notes: Recalled; verse numbering per the common 14-verse division.

paraphrase: Even if you have renunciation and bodhicitta, without the wisdom realising the way things are you cannot cut the root of existence; therefore strive in the means of realising dependent arising.
notes: Recalled; verse numbering per the common 14-verse division.

paraphrase: Whoever sees the cause and effect of all phenomena of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as never failing, and destroys every mode of apprehension (of inherent existence), has entered the path that pleases the Buddhas.
notes: Recalled; verse numbering per the common 14-verse division.

paraphrase: As long as the two understandings — of appearances as unfailing dependent arising and of emptiness as free of assertion — seem separate, you have not yet realised the Sage's intent.
notes: Recalled; verse numbering per the common 14-verse division.

paraphrase: When they arise simultaneously, not alternately, and from merely seeing dependent arising as unfailing, certain knowledge destroys every mode of grasping at an object, the analysis of the view is complete.
notes: Recalled; verse numbering per the common 14-verse division.

paraphrase: Moreover, appearance dispels the extreme of existence and emptiness dispels the extreme of non-existence; when you know how emptiness appears as cause and effect, you will not be captivated by extreme views.
notes: Recalled; verse numbering per the common 14-verse division.

paraphrase: When you have understood the essential points of the three principal aspects of the path, rely on solitude, generate the power of effort and quickly accomplish the final goal, my child.
notes: Recalled; verse numbering per the common 14-verse division.

paraphrase: Seeing cause and effect of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as unfailing while destroying all apprehension of inherent existence, and holding the understanding of appearances as dependent arising and of emptiness as free of assertion together, not alternately, is the completion of the analysis of the view.
notes: Summary entry for vv. 10–12 (each also recorded separately).

paraphrase: I bow to the Conqueror who, seeing and teaching dependent arising, is the unsurpassed knower and teacher.
notes: Opening verse, recalled.

paraphrase: Whatever depends on conditions is empty of inherent existence; no teaching is more wondrous than this. Those who take emptiness to contradict dependent arising have not understood the Buddha; for him, emptiness is the very meaning of dependent arising.
notes: Paraphrase of a recurring argument of the poem; not a single verse.

paraphrase: The author tells how, after long searching, he came through the kindness of his teacher to see Nāgārjuna's system clearly by the light of Candrakīrti's commentary, and was filled with faith in the Buddha as teacher of dependent arising.

Because the scriptures themselves differ — some to be taken literally, others requiring interpretation — which is definitive cannot be settled by citing scripture alone (else endless regress); it must be established by stainless reasoning, following the great charioteers Nāgārjuna and Asaṅga.

The Svātantrika hold that phenomena are posited by appearing to a non-defective awareness together with existing by their own character conventionally; the Prāsaṅgika hold that phenomena are posited only by the force of conceptual designation, with no existence from their own side even conventionally — this is the subtle difference in the object of negation.

Commenting on 'for whom emptiness is possible, everything is possible' (MMK 24.14), Tsongkhapa argues that the opponent who charges emptiness with destroying the four truths has it backwards: only because things are empty of inherent existence can arising, ceasing, the truths and the path be posited.
notes: Chapter-level ref.

paraphrase: In commenting on the sixth chapter of the Madhyamakāvatāra, Tsongkhapa sets out the tenets unique to Prāsaṅgika — rejection of a store-consciousness distinct from the six and of reflexive awareness, acceptance of external objects conventionally, and the rest.
notes: Chapter-level ref.

paraphrase: The eight difficult points of the Prāsaṅgika: (1) no store-consciousness distinct from the six consciousnesses; (2) no reflexive awareness; (3) autonomous syllogisms not used to generate the view in another; (4) external objects accepted (conventionally) just as consciousness is; (5) śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas realise the selflessness of phenomena; (6) grasping at the self of phenomena is an affliction; (7) disintegration (zhig pa) is a functioning thing; (8) hence a unique presentation of the three times.
notes: Recalled list; some presentations give the eighth point as the way a buddha knows conventional phenomena.

paraphrase: Khedrup Je argues that the object of negation must be precisely identified and that Madhyamaka reasoning negates inherent existence, not conventional existence; he criticises other Tibetan readings of the view.
notes: Summary-level, recalled.

paraphrase: Each topic of the stages of the path is sung as Tsongkhapa's own practice, closing with the refrain: 'I, the yogi, have practised in this way; you who seek liberation, please do the same.'
The kind and venerable teacher is the foundation of all good qualities; seeing that relying on him properly is the root of the path, may I rely on him with great effort.

Avalokiteśvara, great treasure of compassion without object; Mañjuśrī, lord of stainless wisdom; (Vajrapāṇi, destroyer of all māras;) Tsongkhapa, crown jewel of the sages of the Land of Snows — Lobsang Drakpa, I make requests at your feet.
notes: The five-line form; the nine-line form adds Vajrapāṇi and other lines. Wording recalled.

paraphrase: From the heart of the protector of the hundred deities of Tuṣita, on a cloud like fresh white curd, the omniscient Lobsang Drakpa, king of dharma, is invited with his two sons to come to this place.

The Mahāyāna has two divisions, the perfection vehicle and the mantra vehicle; they do not differ in the view of emptiness, which is the same, but in method: the mantra vehicle is distinguished by deity yoga, in which the wisdom realising emptiness itself appears as the deity's body.
Entry into the mantra path requires empowerment from a qualified master and the keeping of the tantric vows and pledges; without them, practice produces no attainment and leads to downfall.

In Highest Yoga Tantra the generation stage, visualising oneself and the environment as the deity and maṇḍala to purify ordinary appearance and conception, ripens the continuum for the completion stage, which works on the winds, channels and drops to manifest the clear light and the illusory body.
notes: Summary only; completion-stage methods are restricted.

paraphrase: Following Nāgārjuna's Five Stages, the Guhyasamāja completion stage proceeds through isolation of body, speech and mind, the illusory body, the clear light and union.
notes: Structure only; restricted completion-stage content not recorded.

paraphrase: The six yogas are to be practised only after the common path, a complete empowerment and the generation stage; inner heat is the foundation stone of the completion stage, and wind practices done without instruction and preparation cause illness of the winds.
notes: The text's own cautions, recalled in substance only; no method recorded.

paraphrase: Mahāmudrā is approached in two ways: the sūtra approach, meditating on emptiness as taught by Nāgārjuna and his followers, and the mantra approach, the clear light of great bliss arising when the winds enter, abide and dissolve in the central channel through skilful means.

Resting on the mind itself, the meditator finds it to be mere clarity and awareness, without form, in which anything can appear; then, examining that very mind, finds it lacking inherent existence — its conventional nature is clarity and knowing, its ultimate nature emptiness.

Though many names are given — co-emergent union, the amulet box, the fivefold, one taste, the four letters, pacification, cutting, the great perfection, the Madhyamaka instruction on the view — when examined by a yogin learned in scripture and reasoning and experienced in practice, they come down to one intent.
notes: Recalled; the list of names may differ in order and detail.

paraphrase: The Mahāmudrā taught by the Buddha is the wisdom born of empowerment and the meditative absorption of the two stages; apart from this, the Buddha did not teach any other Mahāmudrā.
notes: Chapter-level ref (the tantric-vows chapter); wording recalled.

paraphrase: The Mahāmudrā of the present day and the Great Perfection of the Chinese tradition differ only in name — 'descending from above' and 'ascending from below', 'simultaneous' and 'gradual' — not in meaning.
notes: Chapter-level ref; the comparison is with the teaching attributed to Hwashang (Moheyan) at the Samye debate.

paraphrase: A fool's meditation on Mahāmudrā usually becomes a cause for rebirth as an animal; if not, one is born in the formless realm, or else falls into the cessation of the śrāvakas; the 'white self-sufficient remedy' (a single realisation said to suffice alone) is not the Buddha's teaching.

paraphrase: The three vows — of individual liberation, of bodhisattvas and of the mantra vehicle — must each be understood and kept according to its own rites and rules; mixing their procedures, or practising rites not found in the scriptures, is not the dharma.

The Sage's intent is the Mahāyāna path: awakening the potential (gotra), going for refuge, generating bodhicitta, and training in the six perfections — with calm and insight as the last two — through the grounds and paths to buddhahood.

paraphrase: Only particulars, which can perform functions, are ultimately (i.e. really) existent; universals are mere conceptual constructs made by the exclusion of what is other, not real entities as the earlier Tibetan logicians held.

paraphrase: A king is honoured only in his own land; a holy person of learning is honoured wherever he goes.

paraphrase: The learned are known through three activities: composition, exposition and debate; each has its rules — for composition, grammar and poetics; for exposition, the proper explanation of a text; for debate, the correct method of proof and refutation.

In Tibet three views are held to be Madhyamaka: the Madhyamaka of the eternalist extreme (Dolpopa: the ultimate is empty of other but not of itself), the Madhyamaka of the nihilist extreme (Tsongkhapa: the ultimate is the mere negation of true existence), and the Madhyamaka free from extremes, which is the view of the Sakya and of Nāgārjuna.

The ultimate is freedom from all elaborations — from the four extremes of existence, non-existence, both and neither; the negation of true existence alone is only a step, and clinging to emptiness as a mere negation is itself an extreme to be abandoned.

Tsongkhapa's addition of the qualifier 'inherently' or 'truly' to the object of negation is not found in Nāgārjuna and Candrakīrti, who negate arising, existence and the rest without qualification; by leaving conventional things unnegated at the level of ultimate analysis, that system clings to a subtle existence.
notes: Summary-level; recalled.

paraphrase: The ultimate truth is not an object of knowledge in the ordinary sense: it is beyond the scope of mind and words; ultimate truth is 'known' only in the sense that, in meditative equipoise, subject and object are no longer divided.

The common Lamdre path is taught under the three visions: under the impure vision, the sufferings of saṃsāra, the difficulty of obtaining leisure and endowment, death and impermanence, and karma and its results, to turn the mind from this life and from saṃsāra; under the experiential vision, love, compassion and bodhicitta, relative and ultimate, and the experiences that arise in meditation; under the pure vision, the qualities of buddhahood, to inspire effort.
notes: Order and grouping of topics recalled with moderate confidence.

paraphrase: The uncommon Lamdre is the three continua: the causal continuum, the all-base as the union of clarity and emptiness in which saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are inseparable; the method continuum, the practices of empowerment and the two stages that ripen and liberate; and the result continuum, Mahāmudrā.

The Kadam practitioner is to hold the seven divine dharmas: the four deities — Śākyamuni as the teacher, Avalokiteśvara as the deity of compassion, Tārā as the protectress of activity, Acala as the guardian against obstacles — and the three baskets as the teaching.

The sixteen drops (thig le bcu drug) of the Kadam: a guru-yoga meditation in which the practitioner visualises nested spheres containing the lineage teachers and deities, culminating in the drop of awakening, as the heart practice of the Kadam oral instructions.

paraphrase: Meditation on selflessness by four essential points: identifying the object of negation (the self as it appears to the innate self-grasping); ascertaining that if such a self existed it would have to be either one with the aggregates or different from them; ascertaining that it is not one; and ascertaining that it is not different.
